title: Dissent and Resistance
theme: Protest, power and resistance in history
objectives: I can explain how people challenge authority and how authorities push back, using ten history words.
I can tell the two meanings of sanction apart by reading the context.
I can turn verbs such as suppress and abolish into nouns and spell them correctly.
I can write a reasoned paragraph about when protest is justified, using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Eighth-grade history texts keep returning to the same conflict: someone in power makes a rule, and someone else says no. The ten words split into the ways people resist (dissent, boycott, strike, activist), the ways authority pushes back (censor, suppress, persecute, tyranny), and the words for what resistance aims at or provokes (abolish, sanction). Sanction is chosen on purpose: it is a rare word that can mean a penalty or an approval, so students must read context rather than guess. Several words also give practice with noun suffixes (-ship, -ion, -ist) and spelling changes, which prepares students for the dense nominalizations in high school social studies.

words.def: Open disagreement with an official decision, a rule, or a widely held opinion.
words.ex: The judge wrote a dissent explaining why she disagreed with the court's decision.
words.ex2: A free society allows citizens to voice dissent without fear of arrest.
words.nonExample: Quietly following a rule you privately dislike is not dissent until you say so out loud.

apps.academic: In a court case, a dissent records why one judge disagreed with the majority.
apps.spoken: I want to voice a little dissent here: I think the first plan was better.
apps.writing: Use dissent for disagreement that is spoken or recorded, and name the authority being challenged.

words.def: To ban or cut out parts of books, news, films, or speech because those in power dislike them.

words.def: Cruel and unfair rule by a person or small group holding unlimited power.

words.ex2: Some writers warn that tyranny can grow slowly when people stop questioning those in power.
words.nonExample: A student council elected by classmates and bound by written rules is not a tyranny.

apps.academic: Political thinkers have long asked how a society can protect itself from tyranny.
apps.spoken: Making everyone obey with no say at all is tyranny.

words.def: To treat a person or group cruelly and unfairly, over time, because of who they are or what they believe.
words.ex: Rulers in many eras persecuted religious minorities, forcing families to hide their beliefs or flee.
words.ex2: The regime persecuted journalists who reported on corruption, jailing some and threatening others.
words.nonExample: Disagreeing with someone's opinion in a debate is not persecuting that person.

misuse.why: To persecute is to mistreat unfairly; granting rights and protection is the opposite.

words.def: To officially end a law, a practice, or a system.
words.ex: After years of petitions, the town council voted to abolish the unfair fee.
words.ex2: Reformers in the nineteenth century campaigned to abolish child labor in factories and mines.
words.nonExample: Changing the wording of a rule is not the same as abolishing it.

apps.academic: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in the United States in 1865.
apps.spoken: Some people want to abolish homework, but others disagree.
apps.writing: Abolish is stronger than reduce, so use it only when something is ended completely.

misuse.why: To abolish is to end something completely; extending and tightening it does the opposite.

words.def: A penalty, such as a trade ban, used to pressure a country or person to follow rules.

words.ex: The state announced sanctions against the company, including a fine and a ban on city contracts.
words.ex2: Several nations imposed economic sanctions until the government agreed to free the prisoners.
words.nonExample: A teacher's friendly reminder to arrive on time is not a sanction.

apps.academic: Economic sanctions are meant to pressure a government without using military force.
apps.spoken: The league imposed a sanction on the team for breaking the rules.
apps.writing: Sanction can mean a penalty or an approval, so check the context before you use it.

passage.title: Saying No to Power
paras: Every society contains people who disagree with its rules. Dissent, the open expression of that disagreement, can be as small as a letter to the editor or as large as a march of thousands. In history, dissent has often been the first step toward change, and those in power have often tried to silence it.

Rulers have many tools for doing so. Some censor books, newspapers, and broadcasts, cutting out ideas they dislike before the public can read them. Others suppress protests by banning meetings or arresting organizers. Under a tyranny, where one person or a small group holds power without limits, such tools are used daily, and people may be persecuted simply for what they believe.

Dissenters have answered with tools of their own. A boycott, in which people refuse to buy from or use a business or service, turns everyday choices into protest. In 1955, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, began a boycott of the city's buses that lasted more than a year and helped end segregated seating. Workers use the strike, a planned stop in work meant to force an employer to meet their demands, to show that the work cannot go on without them.

Pressure sometimes comes from outside a country. Governments may impose sanctions, such as limits on trade, to punish another government for actions they oppose. In the twentieth century, many nations used sanctions against South Africa's system of apartheid, while activists elsewhere urged their own leaders to join in. An activist is someone who works publicly and persistently for political or social change, whether by petition, speech, or organizing.

Activists have also campaigned to abolish laws and practices they judged unjust. In Britain, decades of petitions and speeches, along with a sugar boycott by many families in the 1790s, helped build the pressure that led Parliament to pass a law in 1833 to abolish slavery across most of the British Empire.

None of these methods is free of risk. Dissent can cost people their jobs, their freedom, or their safety. Yet historians observe that societies that protect the right to dissent give themselves a way to correct their own mistakes.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word “boycott” refers to
choices: marching through the streets to demand a new law
refusing to buy or use something as a form of protest
a decision by a court that ends a policy
a planned stop in work by employees
qs.why: The passage defines a boycott as people refusing to buy from or use a business or service. The planned work stoppage is a strike.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, a government that “suppresses” protests is trying to
choices: plan better protests than its critics
encourage them so they will grow
make them more peaceful
stop them from growing or being heard
qs.why: The sentence gives the examples of banning meetings and arresting organizers, both of which aim to stop protests.

qs.q: According to the passage, how is a strike different from a boycott?
choices: A strike is a stop in work by employees, while a boycott is a refusal by customers or riders to use a service.
A strike is always illegal, but a boycott never is.
A strike is organized by governments, while a boycott is organized by employers.
A strike is aimed at other countries, while a boycott is aimed at schools.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 describes the boycott as refusing to buy or use, and the strike as a planned stop in work by workers.

qs.q: Why does the author mention both the Montgomery bus boycott and the British campaign against slavery?
choices: To prove that no protest can succeed without help from another country
To show that boycotts were invented in the 1950s
To show that peaceful pressure has helped change unjust laws in different times and places
To explain why governments should censor the news
qs.why: The two examples come from different centuries and countries, and each shows ordinary people using pressure that helped end an unjust practice.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Rulers who censor the news always lose power quickly.
Dissent has driven change throughout history, even though those in power have tried to stop it and it carries real risk.
Sanctions are the most effective form of protest ever used.
Only large crowds can bring about changes in the law.
qs.why: The passage opens with dissent leading to change, describes how power pushes back and how dissenters respond, and closes on the risk and the value of protecting it.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that describe how people challenge power and how power responds, practice reading sanction in two opposite senses, work with noun suffixes (-ist, -ship, -ion) and a spelling change, and apply the words to a short history passage. The unit follows the ethics and testimony work earlier in the year and prepares for the technology and consequences units.

notes.va.dissent.n: Dissent is open disagreement. Students often treat it as only a negative; point out that a judge's written dissent is a formal, respected document. Have students spot the noun and verb forms: the dissent, to dissent.
notes.va.boycott.n: A boycott is a refusal, so it works by withholding something. The word comes from the name of Captain Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent whom tenants shunned in 1880; share that story only if students are curious. Ask what a boycott needs to work: numbers, a clear goal, and an alternative.
notes.va.strike.n: Strike is a multiple-meaning word; set the hitting sense next to the labor sense on the board. A strike is planned and has demands. Ask students why a sick-out and a strike are different.
notes.va.activist.n: Activist is active plus -ist, a person who does or supports something. Students often think activists must be famous; ask them to find a local one. Distinguish activist from protester: an activist works over time.
notes.va.censor.v: Censor names the power to decide what others may read or say. Be balanced: people disagree about when, if ever, it is justified, so use the word to analyze rather than to settle the question. Link to the noun censorship.
notes.va.suppress.v: Suppress is sup- (a form of sub-, under) plus press. The unit teaches the stop-by-force sense; the feeling sense (suppress a laugh) is shown as a second sense so students are not caught by it. Contrast with repress and oppress if students ask.
notes.va.tyranny.n: Tyranny means unlimited and unfair power, so a strict but accountable leader is not a tyrant. Students overuse the word for any rule they dislike; ask what has to be missing (limits, a voice, a way to challenge).
notes.va.persecute.v: Persecute is mistreatment over time of a group or belief. Do not let students confuse it with prosecute (to bring legal charges). Write both on the board with a sentence each. Handle examples with care and avoid asking students to role-play persecution.
notes.va.abolish.v: Abolish is stronger than reduce: it ends something completely. Connect to abolition and abolitionist for the history of slavery in the United States and Britain. Ask what the opposite word would be.
notes.va.sanction.n: Sanction is a contronym: it can mean penalty or approval. Never accept a definition without a sentence. Give students four sentences and have them mark each as penalty or approval from context. The same two meanings exist for the Spanish sanción.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The text says the government cut out articles it disliked, so that is censoring. It banned meetings and arrested leaders, so that is suppressing, because it is stopping an action. When I read sanction, I do not guess; I look at the words around it. Trade limits meant to pressure a country, so it is a penalty here.”

Fact claims in the passage to confirm: the Montgomery boycott lasted more than a year (about 381 days) and helped end segregated bus seating; many nations used sanctions against South Africa's apartheid system; British families boycotted slave-grown sugar in the 1790s; Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833 covering most of the empire; the Thirteenth Amendment of 1865.

Sense boundaries: strike (labor sense taught; hitting sense shown as a second sense), suppress (stop by force taught; hold back a feeling shown as a second sense), sanction (penalty taught; approval shown as a second sense).
